# 5 Rationalistic Criticisms

Messrs.[^1] Schiller's and Dewey's theories have suffered a hailstorm of contempt and ridicule.[^2] All rationalism has risen against them.[^3] A hailstorm of contempt and ridicule[^4] throws so much sidelight upon that rationalistic temper to which I, William James,[^5] have opposed the temper of pragmatism.[^6] Pragmatism is uncomfortable away from facts.[^7] Rationalism is comfortable only in the presence of abstractions.[^8] This pragmatist talk about truths in the plural, about their utility and satisfactoriness, about the success with which they 'work,' etc., suggests to the typical intellectualist mind a sort of coarse lame second-rate makeshift article of truth.[^9] Such truths are not real truth.[^10] Such tests are merely subjective.[^11] As against this, objective truth must be something non-utilitarian, haughty, refined, remote, august, exalted.[^12] It must be an absolute correspondence of our thoughts with an equally absolute reality.[^13] It must be what we OUGHT to think, unconditionally.[^14] The conditioned ways in which we DO think are so much irrelevance and matter for psychology.[^15] Down with psychology, up with logic, in all this question![^16]

The pragmatist clings to facts and concreteness, observes truth at its work in particular cases, and generalizes.[^17] Truth, for him, becomes a class-name for all sorts of definite working-values in experience.[^18] For the rationalist it remains a pure abstraction, to the bare name of which we must defer.[^19] When the pragmatist undertakes to show in detail just WHY we must defer, the rationalist is unable to recognize the concretes from which his own abstraction is taken.[^20] He accuses us,[^21] Messrs.[^22] Dewey, Schiller and their allies,[^23] of DENYING truth; whereas we have only sought to trace exactly why people follow it and always ought to follow it.[^24] Your typical ultra-abstractionist fairly shudders at concreteness: other things equal, he positively prefers the pale and spectral.[^25]

Pragmatism[^26] only follows here the example of the sister-sciences, interpreting the unobserved by the observed.[^27] It brings old and new harmoniously together.[^28] It converts the absolutely empty notion of a static relation of 'correspondence'[^29] between our minds and reality, into that of a rich and active commerce (that anyone may follow in detail and understand) between particular thoughts of ours, and the great universe of other experiences in which they play their parts and have their uses.[^30]
